summary: Fine-tuning makes sense when you need to change a model's intrinsic behavior, tone, or domain fluency, or when you want to compress long, repetitive prompts into learned weights for latency and cost gains at scale. RAG is the better choice when the problem is access to fresh or proprietary knowledge that changes over time, while prompt engineering should be exhausted first because it is the cheapest and fastest to iterate on. In practice, teams often combine a lightly fine-tuned base model with RAG for knowledge grounding.
when_to_fine_tune: Choose fine-tuning when you need consistent output format, style, or domain tone that prompting alone cannot reliably enforce across thousands of calls.
Prefer fine-tuning over RAG when the task is about teaching new skills or behaviors rather than injecting changing factual knowledge.
Fine-tune to reduce latency and token costs by baking repetitive instructions into the model weights at high request volumes.
Avoid fine-tuning when your data changes frequently or you need source citations — use RAG instead, and start with prompt engineering whenever possible.
